titleStmt.title: Hybrid Algorithms for Dynamic Schedulability Testing

analytic.title: Hybrid Algorithms for Dynamic Schedulability Testing

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper describes an investigation into the performance of a variety of algorithms for dynamic schedulability testing. A real-time node may run its own set of resident periodic tasks and may also receive aperiodic requests for computations to be completed within hard deadlines. In order to decide whether each request is schedulable, and can therefore be accepted, the node may use a guarantee algorithm. Such algorithms trade off complexity against pessimism. This paper describes how algorithms of hybrid complexity can achieve the best trade-off for given characteristics of the resident periodic task set.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Many real-time applications require distributed processors with tasks which are required to meet hard deadlines. According to the Spring Project [ll] such real-time systems will be complex and will need to adapt to environmental changes, maintenance requirements, system faults, etc. Consequently dynamic scheduling is required in order to provide load-shanng and a flexible use of processors. A processor should therefore be able to schedule not only its resident tasks but also any aperiodic tasks which arrive from the environment or other parts of the system. The problem of scheduling both aperiodic and resident periodic tasks has been tackled at various levels of sophistication. The crudest method is simply to run the aperiodics in background with no regard to their criticality. Better, is to invent a polling task which runs periodically and uses its large capacity to service periodics. All tasks can then be scheduled, for example, according to the rate monotonic scheduling algorithm as shown by Lui and Layland [7].

Obviously an aperiodic which arrives just after the polling task has run will have to wait a maximum time for it to run again. Improvements on this are the sporadic server due to Sprunt [lo], and the deferrable server due 1068-3070/95 $4.00 0 1995 IEEE to Strosnider [13] which allow the server task's capacity to be used throughout the server's period. Each of these has a different schedulability analysis which must be carried out if the aperiodic is to be guaranteed to meet a hard deadline. However, these methods do not take advantage of spare capacity which arises at run time when tasks compiete in less than their worst-case execution time.

The Spring Project has a different method of dealing with aperiodic tasks. A Spring node has a set of resident periodic tasks which are guaranteed schedulable before run-time. An aperiodic task with a hard deadline which arrives at a Spring node will be tested for schedulability along with the resident set of (hard) periodic tasks. The node's guarantee algorithm [12] will use run-time data to attempt to construct a schedule which includes the extra task, and may also take into account resources and task precedence constraints. If a schedule cannot be constructed, the aperiodic cannot be guaranteed, and an attempt may be made to offload the task to another processor which may be able to guarantee it. The drawback is the large overhead introduced by the construction of a schedule which guarantees the aperiodic.

Other approaches such as Leung and Whitehead [6] are aimed at fixed-priority tasks in deadline monotonic ordering which is an optimal scheduling method even when a task's deadline is less than its period. For example have developed a slack stealing algorithm. When an aperiodic task arrives at a node the algorithm tries to steal time from the resident tasks without causing their deadlines to be missed. The slack stealer provides optimal service for aperiodic tasks by delaying the periodic tasks as long as possible until they have just sufficient time left to meet their deadlines. have extended their slack stealer to guarantee aperiodics with hard deadlines. As with Spring, the problem is that the overhead for the guarantee test is considerable. The tests make the worst-case critical instant assumption that all tasks are released simultaneously. Both tests guarantee tasks, but one test is pessimistic and simple (Om2)) while the other is optimal and pseudopolynomial (henceforth referred to as PP). This paper details an attempt to adapt Audsley's algorithms for dynamic use. The intention is to provide a rival dynamic schedulability test to that of Spring or Lehoczky.

However, it is hoped that the overheads incurred by this test will be more acceptable. It is assumed throughout that the overheads of dynamic schedulability testing can be bounded i.e. that aperiodic tasks have minimum interarrival times and are sporadic tasks.

div.head: Algorithms for Dynamic Testing
div.p: Pre-emptive fixed-priority scheduling is widely used in real-time systems due to its combination of predictability and flexibility. It simplifies real-time kernels and its use of priorities facilitates bounds on task blocking. Furthermore, the priority scheme has been chosen by the programming language Ada. The problem addressed in this paper is how to provide the computationally cheapest method of guaranteeing the schedulability of a set of N fixed-priority tasks. Guarantees must be performed dynamically in order for the resident task set to include a newly arrived sporadic. Audsley [l] discusses two algorithms for static schedulability testing: Om2) and PP. Audsley assumes a set of tasks ranked in priority order according to deadline monotonic ordering. The period (T), deadline (0) and worst-case execution time (C) of each task is known. It is assumed that all tasks are released simultaneously (worst-case critical instant). The Om2) algorithm may include interference which does not occur during the lapsed execution time of the test task. Hence this test is sufficient but not necessary. Note that all those tasks which fall below the sporadic in the list must also be schedulability tested to ensure that they can still meet their deadlines. div.head: Simulation Studies
div.p: Simulation studies of the dynamic algorithms were performed using co-operative, fixed-priority pre-emptive scheduling. The schedulability testing part of the simulation ran in real time in order to measure exactly the overheads incurred by each algorithm. The processor used was a T800 transputer. The slot size of the cooperative scheduler was lOms and it was decided that a sporadic request would be automatically rejected if a schedulability test exceeded this time. The minimum interarrival time of sporadic tasks was set to 100ms. Performance was measured by the guarantee ratio which is the proportion of the total number of sporadic requests which pass their schedulability test and are accepted.

Before guarantee ratios could be measured by a simulation, upper bounds for the times taken to run each schedulability test algorithm had to be found. These were schedulability testing rapidly increase as the number of periodics below the sporadic increases. This explains why the guarantee ratios for most algorithms fall off as N increases. The following is a commentary on the results shown in Graph 1.

Om2) shows a low guarantee ratio at N = 5 which is due to its greater pessimism for small sets of periodic tasks with large computation times. The dip in guarantee ratio at N = 15 can be explained by the random effect of this pessimism. For PP the schedulability testing overheads increase rapidly as N increases. This explains the sharp decline in guarantee ratio for PP when N is high. Conversely, at low N and with low schedulability testing overheads, a high guarantee ratio is obtained for equal to the worst-case execution times for the high priority periodic which modelled schedulability testing itself. The simulations actually used these worst-case execution times when performing schedulability tests on incoming sporadics. The iterative method used to obtain each upper bound was to repeatedly run the simulation until the maximum schedulability test time generated was just less than the upper bound which had been set for that simulation.

The results in Graph 1 show the average guarantee ratio obtained in simulation runs for various schedulability test algorithms. Processor utilisation of the resident periodic task sets was constant at 85%. Sporadic arrivals were Poisson distributed, and if all were accepted this would add approximately 10% to the processor utilisation. This is because the overheads for PP because it is an exact test. In other words O(N2) and PP algorithms make complementary trade-offs between complexity and exactness. This argues that an algorithm of hybrid complexity which combines O(N2) and PP might give a more consistent performance when N is varied. Such a hybrid algorithm could perform the Om2) test first. Only if this test fails need the algorithm invoke PP. Hence this algorithm sRould be both exact and faster, on average, than PP.

Graph 1 confirms that Hybrid does indeed produce a better performance profile, except at N = 30 where the overheads of the PP component still have a considerable effect. In fact the lOms timeout was required at N = 30 in order to obtain a guarantee ratio as high as that shown in Graph 1. An enhancement of the hybrid algorithm was to reverse the order of schedulability testing by starting with the lowest priority task first and then working up the task list until the sporadic itself was schedulability tested. Named Bottom-up Hybrid, this algorithm gave the best overall profile of all the algorithms shown in Graph 1. This can be explained by the greater likelihood of an unschedulable task being found lower down the task list. In other words, those schedulability tests which will eventually fail are being abandoned earlier by the bottom-up order of testing.

Background is included for comparison purposes. This algorithm does not guarantee tasks but simply executes them in FIFO order, at the lowest priority. It also deletes sporadics from the task list once their deadlines have expired. The proportions of sporadics which turn out to meet their deadlines under Background scheduling are given by the Success Ratios shown in Graph 1.

Graphs 2 and 3 show the comparative performance of the five algorithms when other parameters are varied. Graph 2 compares performance when the periodc utilisation is varied from 65% up to 85%. Sporadic arrival rates were Poisson distributed, as in Graph 1. Lower utilisations are not shown because they cause the performance of all of the algorithms to converge at a guarantee ratio of unity. All other parameters were kept constant (e.g. N = IO). Graph 3 shows the effect of varying the sporadic utilisation. This was done by adopting a uniform (rather than Poisson) arrival rate which varied from 0.0004 to 0.01 sporadics per millisecond. This gave sporadic utilisations from 1% to 25%. Periodic utilisation was 85% and N = 10. These graphs show the algorithms conforming to similar performance profiles. Again Bottom-up Hybrid consistently outperforms all the other algorithms. Bottom-up Hybrid was therefore chosen as the most efficient algorithm. However Bottom-up Hybrid can still incur overheads in excess of 10 ms when N > 20. Therefore the next objective was to attempt to optimise Bottom-up Hybrid. These attempts are described in the following sections, Hybrid is referred to as Pure BUH.

div.head: Improving the PP component
div.p: Firstly, attempts were made to optimise the PP component of Pure BUH. In order to reduce the number of iterations and thus the overhead of PP, a possible optimisation was to initialise the interference window wi to some value which is larger than the computational requirement of the test task, i. Instead the window could be initialised to the value of the following expression which can be regarded as a 'Headstart' :

div.p: In other words the initial Headstart is the sum of the interferences of each higher priority task, j , (up to its floor value) plus the computational requirement of the test task, i. Unfortunately this turns PP into a suf6cient but not necessary test. PP becomes pessimistic because the initial window considered may be too large, and therefore include more interferences from higher priority tasks than is actually the case when a schedule is constructed. PP may then increase the window until the deadline of the test task is exceeded. For examples of this see McElhone [9]. This first attempt was called Original Headstart. Further variations on Headstart were attempted in order to make it less pessimistic.

The second version of Headstart calculated the lowest floor of all the interfering higher priority tasks. This is then taken as the initial value of the window in which the higher priority tasks may interfere. Therefore for a test task, i, the initial window would be:

div.p: The idea was to avoid the inclusion of extra interferences which occur in the latter part of the deadline interval of the test task. Note that this incurs the extra overhead of a preliminary search for the lowest floor. This method is referred to as Minimum Headstart. One problem is that the lowest floor could be so low as to nulllfy any optimising effect on PP. Also this amendment to Headstart is stili sufficient but not necessary. In fact McElhone [9] shows that, in general, the slack required by the test task may occur at an arbitrarily early point.

Therefore, to set the initial window to any more than the computational requirement of the test task may lead to the test task pessimistically failing the schedulability test. Nevertheless it was decided to simulate Headstart because, even though it provides a pessimistic test, it could still increase the throughput of sporadic tasks by cutting down time spent on schedulability testing. Furthermore, any headstart may reduce the worst-case bound for the schedulability test and this itself may allow more tasks to be guaranteed.

A final variation was BUH with Average Headstart. This was an attempt to find the "best of both worlds" from Original and Minimum Headstart. The initial interference window is set to halfthe value of the test task's deadline. The hope was that this might strike an optimum balance between the pessimism of Original Headstart and the larger overhead of Minimum Headstart.

Graph 4 shows the results of headstart investigations. Pure BUH is included in the graph for comparison purposes. PP with Original Headstart shows the effect of Headstart on pure PP without any OW2) component. The resulting performance is much the same pure PP. At small N this algorithm gives high guarantee ratios, but guarantee ratio rapidly declines as N increases, until at N = 30 guarantee ratio is virtually zero (not shown on graph). As expected, BUH with Original Headstart gives a better performance at high N than PP with Original Headstart. It is worth comparing Pure BUH with BUH with Original Headstart. For low N both algorithms give very similar results. However there are differences at N = 20 and N = 30. At N = 20 Pure BUH performs better, whereas at N = 30 it performs worse. This can be interpreted as the effect of the pessimism of BUH with Original Headstart showing at N = 20.
However, at N = 30, the lower average schedulability testing times obtained with BUH with Original Headstart are more significant.

BUH with Minimum Headstart performs closely to Pure BUH, except for a modest improvement at N = 10, and a deterioration at N = 30. The deterioration at high N can be explained as follows. For a large number of tasks, it is more likely that the lowest of the floors is near to the current time at which schedulability testing is taking place. In this case Minimum Headstart algorithm degenerates to Pure BUR, except that it still incurs the extra overhead of finding the lowest floor among higher priority tasks.

BUH with Average Headstart, performs best only at N = 30. This can be explained as follows. For each test task i which is to be schedulability tested, the task list must be traversed downwards, calculating the interferences from all higher priority tasks. Any interference from a higher priority task which overlaps the deadline of the test task can be used to reduce the test task deadline to an effective deadline. The advantage of this is that concurrent interferences from higher priority tasks, occurring near the test task deadline, are not pessimistically included in the total interference within performance. Hence the chances of being pessimistic are marginally increased. (A floor value would exclude the possibility of pessimistically including the whole of a partial hit for the interfering task whose floor it is. An arbitrary time such as half the test task's deadline does not exclude ths possibility.) A general conclusion from these investigations is that Headstart can increase performance at high N, but that its pessimism can reduce performance at low N.

div.head: Improving the O(N2) component
div.p: The second part of the attempt to improve the efficiency of Pure BUH was to increase the exactness of the initial Ow2) component of the algorithm. Audsley's idea of an A final variation uses BUH with Effective Deadline Bound plus Original Headstart for the PP component. The idea here is that the O(N2) component will be made more exact by the use of effective deadline, and the PP component will be made faster by upper-bounding wj by an effective deadline, and lower-bounding it by a headstart. A general conclusion from these results is that the use of Effective Deadline can increase performance when N is small, but that the associated overheads can decrease performance when N is large.

div.head: Dynamic placement of sporadics
div.p: During the above work it was discovered that placing the sporadics within the task list according to a static, deadline monotonic ordering is not an optimal positioning. This is because a sporadic can arrive at arbitrary points within a schedule, and therefore should be placed according to the dynamic values of the remaining deadlines of existing tasks. Therefore to ensure optimality there should be no task below the sporadic which has a shorter dynamic deadline (for proof of this see Davis and Burns [3]). The results shown in Graph 6 show that such optimal placement generally improves guarantee ratios, except when N = 30. This is because at high N optimal placement can increase the average number of tasks below the sporadic position and therefore increases the schedulability testing overhead. It is notable that the relative performances of the algorithms are largely unchanged by the use of optimal placement.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: The following points summarise the main conclusions of this work: Dynamic schedulability testing of sporadic tasks on the same processor as the periodic task set can incur acceptable overheads. An algorithm of hybrid complexity provides greater throughput of sporadic tasks than does one of purely O(N2) or pseudo-polynomial complexity. When the number of tasks in the task list is high, then a pessimistic but faster form of the pseudopolynomial component of the hybrid algorithm can result in a greater throughput of sporadic tasks. When the number of tasks in the task list is low, then it is cost-effective to incur extra overheads in order to make the Om2) component of the hybrid algorithm more exact. The performances of the hybrid algorithms can be increased by the use of optimal placement of sporadic requests instead of static placement by deadline monotonic ordering. However performance can also be decreased when optimal placement results in higher overheads for schedulability testing. The relative performances of the hybrid algorithms are largely unchanged under optimal placement of sporadics. No single one of the hybrid algorithms investigated will perform best for all periodic task sets. In particular, different algorithms may have to be chosen for different sizes of periodic task set.

BUH with Effective Deadline performs better than Pure BUH for low values of N, but the situation is reversed at N = 30. This can be explained by the extra overhead incurred by the use of effective deadline. This overhead increases with N and becomes less cost-effective as it does so. At low N the overhead is worthwhile because it reduces the pessimism of the OW2) component.
